name: Juba Arabic
confidence_why: Manfredi & Petrollino 2013 state a first-heavy-syllable-else-initial stress rule that their own later work (Manfredi & Tosco 2014) softens to an etymological tendency with many exceptions, while Nakao 2017 and Nakao 2021, from independent fieldwork, find a lexically fixed high tone with no syllable-weight condition inside a split accent-and-tone system and reject the accent-language label outright, and no third fieldworker settles it.

catalog_quote: Juba Arabic presents a five vowel set ( a, e, i, o, u). The predominant syllable structure is open, although syllable-internal consonant clusters are also allowed. Stress is phonetically realized as a high pitch and can be distinctive, both lexically and grammatically. ... Vowel quantity is not distinctive, either lexically or grammatically, although long allophonic variants are found in acrolectal registers; vowel length is also predictable in stressed syllables, and it can be prompted by pragmatic factors such as emphasis. ... Stress is confined to the first syllable if there are no heavy syllables, otherwise the first heavy syllable in the word will be stressed. In a few cases stress is lexically distinctive, e.g. sába ‘seven’ vs. sabá ‘morning’, záman ‘when’ vs. zamán ‘ancient times’. In verbal derivation (see §7.1), stress dislocation distinguishes the active (transitive) voice fr…
sweep_summary: suda1237 (Juba Arabic) is in the catalog as weight-sensitive (tentative) / weight-hedged ('first heavy syllable else initial', APiCS survey 64, with Manfredi & Tosco 2014 as supplement). Three target items: (1) Manfredi & Tosco 2014 — already held by the project (HAL preprint, catalog tree) and already the catalog's supplementary source; §2.1 gives one pitch accent per word, lexically and grammatically contrastive, position 'etymologically determined by the vowel length' with 'many exceptions' — refines, no new download needed. (2) Kabak & Lorenzen 2020 — Crossref abstract shows it is about spoken Turkish suffix stress; Glottolog misattribution; irrelevant. (3) Nakao 2013 (De Gruyter, pp. not read; priority high, though its substance (split pitch accent + tone system) is restated first-hand in two open Nakao texts already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 search: the 2021 ILCAA chapter (Japanese, CC BY, 24 pp.) and the 2017 Kyoto thesis abstract/digest (full thesis not public — repository holds only the two summary PDFs, verified via the DSpace API). Best new statement = Nakao 2021 pp. 68, 76–77, 84: one lexically specified H (or final F) per word in Arabic-derived words, verbs with word-initial H (passive = final H, verbal noun = penult H), substrate/slang words with syllable-by-syllable tone; no weight rule; JA 'cannot simply be called an accent language'. This contradicts the weight-sensitive coding and supports a lexical / tonal-OR-pitch accent reclassify (the alternative already flagged); recommend at minimum adding Nakao 2021 as the counter-analysis of record. Also held by the project but not read this search of works with stress in the title: Caron, Lux, Manfredi & Pereira 2015 (intonation of topic/focus; sentence prosody by title). Files (new: two Internet Archive copy of the Nakao 2013 landing page, Crossref/Unpaywall JSON for Nakao 2013 and Kabak & Lorenzen 2020). discovery was done through Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, the Kyoto/TUFS repository APIs, Google Books API and the Internet Archive instead.

new_statements.quote: ジュバ・アラビア語ではアラビア語的なアクセント・システム（語彙的に指定される韻律的な卓立）と、アフリカ諸語的なトーン・システムが共存する、分裂的なプロソディ・システムが形成されている (Nakao 2013, 2017)。[p. 68] … 一語中に一ヶ所のみ H ないし F（太字で示す）をもつパタンに当てはまる語が大部分である。これは、語彙供給言語であるアラビア語スーダン方言（一般的にはストレス・アクセント言語であると言われる）のアクセント・パタンが反映されたものである。[pp. 76–77] … ジュバ・アラビア語の動詞は（極めて少数のスラング動詞を除き）全ての動詞はアクセント語類に属し、かつ大部分の動詞は音節数に関わらず語頭音節に H（1 音節語の場合は H または F）をもつ。[p. 84]
new_statements.translation: In Juba Arabic a split prosodic system has formed in which an Arabic-type accent system (lexically specified prosodic prominence) coexists with an African-type tone system (Nakao 2013, 2017). [p. 68] … The great majority of words fit pattern (12), i.e. have only one H or F per word; this reflects the accent pattern of the lexifier, Sudanese Arabic (generally said to be a stress-accent language). [pp. 76–77] … All Juba Arabic verbs (except a very few slang verbs) belong to the accent word-class, and most verbs have H on the word-initial syllable regardless of the number of syllables (H or F for monosyllables). [p. 84]
new_statements.citation: 仲尾周一郎 [Nakao, Shuichiro]. 2021. 第4章 ジュバ・アラビア語におけるトーンのふるまい [The behaviour of tone in Juba Arabic]. In 梶茂樹 (ed.), アフリカ諸語の声調・アクセント = Tone and Accent in African Languages, 67–90. Tokyo: ILCAA (CC BY 4.0; DOI 10.15026/99915; hdl 10108/99915).
new_statements.locator: p. 68 (§1); pp. 76–77 (§3, pattern (12)); p. 84 (§4.4 動詞とトーンのふるまい); summary (35) pp. 88–89
new_statements.reading: Nakao's first-hand analysis (2010–2013 Juba fieldwork, restating his 2013 De Gruyter chapter and 2017 Kyoto grammar): the word prominence is a lexically specified H (or word-final F) tone, one per word in most Arabic-derived words, at a position fixed per lexeme (near-minimal pairs at every syllable position, (1) p. 69); verbs carry word-initial H, with passive = H on the final syllable (kasurú) and verbal noun = H on the penult (kasúru); Bari/substrate-derived and slang words carry syllable-by-syllable tone. No syllable-weight rule of any kind is stated, and he explicitly concludes JA 'cannot simply be called an accent language' (p. 89). This contradicts the catalog's weight-hedged 'first heavy syllable else initial' rule (which also rests on an undefined 'heavy' in a language with non-distinctive vowel length) and supports the lexical / tonal-OR-pitch accent alternative that already flagged as arguable. Manfredi & Tosco 2014 fn. 2 themselves record Nakao's competing analysis; the Kyoto examiners' digest (2017) endorses the pitch accent-plus-tone finding.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Agree, and the source is stronger than the report states. Nakao does not merely omit a weight rule; he states one negatively: (11c) p. 76 音節の重さ（開音節か閉音節か）によって現れうるトーンの多様性が変わらない ('the range of tones that can occur does not change with syllable weight, open vs closed'), alongside (11b) 明白な H・L トーンの分布の制約が見られない ('no obvious constraint on the distribution of H/L'). tone_statements.citation: Lang, Jürgen. 2023. Juba Arabic und Kinubi: Historische Entstehung und afrikanisches Erbe von zwei arabischen Kreolsprachen. Erlangen: FAU University Press. 273 pp. DOI 10.25593/978-3-96147-682-4 (open access; OAPEN hdl 20.500.12657/103741).
tone_statements.quote: Was nun die beiden arabischen Kreols betrifft, so halten Nhial 1975, Nyombe 1986: 77 und Nakao 2013 das JA und Heine 1982: 26/27 das Nubi für eine Tonsprache. … Die hier nicht genannten Autoren sprechen bezüglich des JA und des Nubi nicht von Tönen. Sicher ist aber: der Wortakzent wird in den beiden Kreols eindeutig mehr durch Tonhöhe als durch Lautstärke markiert (vgl. Manfredi/Tosco 2014: 2-3, Watson 2015: 7, Manfredi 2017: 37 und Manfredi/Petrollino 2018: 56) und seine Position kann bedeutungsrelevant sein (vgl. hier 2.3.3.4).
tone_statements.translation: As for the two Arabic creoles, Nhial 1975, Nyombe 1986: 77 and Nakao 2013 consider JA, and Heine 1982: 26/27 Nubi, to be a tone language. … The authors not named here do not speak of tones for JA and Nubi. What is certain, however: in both creoles the word accent is clearly marked more by pitch than by loudness (cf. Manfredi/Tosco 2014: 2-3, Watson 2015: 7, Manfredi 2017: 37 and Manfredi/Petrollino 2018: 56), and its position can be meaning-distinguishing (cf. 2.3.3.4 here).
tone_statements.locator: p. 117, sec. 2.1.1 'Suprasegementales'; see also p. 126 (txt 4675-4678), p. 127 (txt 4714-4720) and Tabelle 16 p. 238 (txt 9022)
tone_statements.summary: Reports that some authors call Juba Arabic tonal, others not; concludes it has a musical word accent: one accent per word realised by pitch, its position distinctive (e.g. passive by final accent).

tone_statements.quote: In the current Youth Juba Arabic, Bari plural suffix -jin with polar tone (e.g. mede-jin ‘school-PL’, cdmd-jin ‘food-PL’), … As aresult of this continuing heavy influence, the prosodic system of Juba Arabic consists of two split parts, very tonal system for African lexicon and pitch-accent system for Arabic lexicon (Nakao, to appear b). Such a split phonological system is ubiquitous among pidgins and creoles.
tone_statements.locator: p. 131, sec. 2.4 'Post-Colonial Period 1950s-2010s', sub-heading 'Expansion of Juba Arabic', + footnote at page foot
tone_statements.summary: States a split prosody, citing his own 2011 paper: pitch accent system for Arabic-derived words, 'very tonal' system for African-derived words; Youth speech has Bari plural -jin with polar tone.

tone_statements.citation: 仲尾周一郎 [Nakao, Shuichiro]. 2011. 現代若年層ジュバ・アラビア語についての予備的報告 [A preliminary report on present-day youth Juba Arabic]. 地球研言語記述論集 / RIHN Descriptive Linguistics Series 3: 59-83. Kyoto: Research Institute for Humanity and Nature, Indus Project.
tone_statements.quote: なお、JA はピッチが弁別的であり、記号 ´ でH (high tone /˥/)、記号 ^ にてF (falling tone /˥˩/)、記号なしでL (low tone /˩/) を示す (e.g. dé /de˥/「これ」、bê /be˥˩/「～もまた」、be /be˩/「～で」)。KA およびMSA はストレスアクセントを持つが、その位置を記号 ˈ にて示す。
tone_statements.translation: Note that in JA pitch is distinctive; the sign ´ marks H (high tone /˥/), the sign ^ marks F (falling tone /˥˩/), and no sign marks L (low tone /˩/) (e.g. dé /de˥/ 'this', bê /be˥˩/ 'also', be /be˩/ 'in, at'). KA and MSA have stress accent, whose position is shown with the sign ˈ.
tone_statements.locator: p. 60, sec. 1.2, note after (2) segment inventories
tone_statements.summary: Pitch is distinctive: high, falling, low (dé 'this', bê 'also', be 'in'); most verbs have initial H prominence; nouns form verbs by moving H to the first syllable; youth bi vs bí differ by pitch only.

tone_statements.citation: Miller, Catherine. 1984. Etude sociolinguistique du développement de l'arabe au Sud Soudan. Thèse de doctorat (3e cycle), Université de la Sorbonne Nouvelle (Paris III), dir. David Cohen. 454 pp. HAL tel-01056017 (open access).
tone_statements.quote: L'accent en Juba arabic est un accent à hauteur et à intensité.On distingue un ton haut et un ton bas, le ton haut coïncide toujours avec la syllabe accentuée. La hauteur de l'accent varie avec la structure syllabique. Les syllabes CY ou CVC accentuée, ont très souvent une tonalité plus haute. La place de l'accent dépend principalement de la structure syllabique du mot. … [p.148:] L'accent n'est pas libre et le système n'a pas glissé vers un système tonal. … Certaines formes comportent un deuxième ‘ton" haut … le rôle de ce.deuxième ton doit être éclairci.
tone_statements.translation: The accent in Juba Arabic is an accent of pitch and of intensity. One distinguishes a high tone and a low tone; the high tone always coincides with the accented syllable. The pitch of the accent varies with syllable structure. Accented CV or CVC syllables very often have a higher pitch. The place of the accent depends mainly on the syllable structure of the word. ... The accent is not free and the system has not slid towards a tonal system. ... Some forms carry a second high 'tone' ... the role of this second tone must be clarified.
tone_statements.locator: thesis p. 138, Part III Phonologie, 'L'accent' (nature de l'accent); and 'Résumé du système accentuel', thesis p. 148
tone_statements.summary: Word accent of pitch and intensity: one accent per word, high tone on the accented syllable, placed by syllable weight; explicitly not a tonal system; a second high tone in some forms unexplained.

audit.recode_to: lexical (classification lexical), matching sister creole Ki-Nubi (nubi1253, coded lexical from Luffin/Gussenhoven): culminative high-pitch accent, one H (or word-final F) per word in the Arabic-derived 'accent word class', position lexically specified (n+1 patterns for n syllables; minimal triplet sáhara 'all-nighter' / sahára 'witch' / sahará 'Sahara'), etymologically continuing Sudanese Arabic stress; verbs default to initial H with grammatical shift (penult = verbal noun, final = passive). Defensible alternative under the catalog's other convention: tonal-OR-pitch accent (Nakao's own analysis: distinctive H/L/F tone, a minority substrate class with free tone). Either way drop weight-sensitive (tentative): no synchronic weight default is supported.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding APiCS passage and the Manfredi & Tosco 2014 supplementary passages are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators (independent the compilers had also confirmed). (2) Deciding source: a 2013 specialist grammar sketch (APiCS survey 64) plus a 2014 prosody/information-structure article; first-hand and competent, but the weight rule is one sentence with 'heavy' undefined in a language the same sketch says has no phonemic vowel length. (3) Better sources exist and are not yet obtained: Nakao 2013 (dedicated prosody chapter, De Gruyter, paywalled), Manfredi 2017 (231-pp Peeters reference grammar, print only), Nakao 2017 Kyoto PhD grammar (full text closed; summary downloaded). Everything openly reachable was downloaded: Caron/Lux/Manfredi/Pereira 2015 (HAL) restates JA as a pitch accent language whose accent position is lexically and grammatically distinctive, with no weigh

Sentence accent = highest lexical pitch accent in the IU. No weight rule stated.

sources.citation: Manfredi, Stefano & Mauro Tosco. 2014. The morphosyntax and prosody of topic and focus in Juba Arabic. Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 29(2): 319–351. (Glottolog 528574; already_listed)
sources.quote: JA is a pitch-accent language (Manfredi and Petrollino 2013: 56). The pitch accent has both lexical and grammatical import and it is marked here with an acute accent. ... Although many exceptions are found, one can say that the positioning of pitch accent in JA is etymologically determined by the vowel length, with Arabic long vowels being reinterpreted as stressed (e.g. *bārid > bárid 'cold'). A word in JA can be phonetically defined as a unit bearing a single pitch accent. [fn. 2:] Nakao (2013), for his part, argues that Juba Arabic posses a split prosodic system in which both pitch accent and tone are lexically and grammatically distinctive.
sources.locator: HAL preprint hal-01102718, section 2.1 'Typological remarks', p. 2 (+ footnote 2); the rest of the article is sentence-level prosody of topic/focus
sources.note: One pitch accent per word, lexically contrastive (záman/zamán, tában/tabán) and grammatically contrastive on verbs (kátulu 'kill' / katúlu VN / katulú PASS; disyllabic jíbu / jibú; ambitransitives like worí final-accented). Position is said to be etymological (Arabic long vowels > accented), with 'many exceptions'; no synchronic weight rule is given. Reports Nakao 2013's competing split pitch accent + tone analysis.

What is certain, however: in both creoles the word accent is clearly marked more by pitch than by loudness (cf. Manfredi/Tosco 2014: 2-3, Watson 2015: 7, Manfredi 2017: 37 and Manfredi/Petrollino 2018: 56), and its position can be meaning-distinguishing (cf. 2.3.3.4 here).

sources.quote: L'accent en Juba arabic est un accent à hauteur et à intensité.On distingue un ton haut et un ton bas, le ton haut coïncide toujours avec la syllabe accentuée. La hauteur de l'accent varie avec la structure syllabique. Les syllabes CY ou CVC accentuée, ont très souvent une tonalité plus haute. La place de l'accent dépend principalement de la structure syllabique du mot. … [p.148:] L'accent n'est pas libre et le système n'a pas glissé vers un système tonal. … Certaines formes comportent un deuxième ‘ton" haut … le rôle de ce.deuxième ton doit être éclairci.

tone.translation: The accent in Juba Arabic is an accent of pitch and of intensity. One distinguishes a high tone and a low tone; the high tone always coincides with the accented syllable. The pitch of the accent varies with syllable structure. Accented CV or CVC syllables very often have a higher pitch. The place of the accent depends mainly on the syllable structure of the word. ... The accent is not free and the system has not slid towards a tonal system. ... Some forms carry a second high 'tone' ... the role of this second tone must be clarified.
tone.summary: Word accent of pitch and intensity: one accent per word, high tone on the accented syllable, placed by syllable weight; explicitly not a tonal system; a second high tone in some forms unexplained.
tone.says: Word accent of pitch and intensity: one accent per word, high tone on the accented syllable, placed by syllable weight; explicitly not a tonal system; a second high tone in some forms unexplained.
